hero.introParagraph: TeleDirectMD treats pediatric pink eye (conjunctivitis, ICD-10 H10.9 and H10.33) by secure video visit for children ages 5 to 17. TeleDirectMD is a physician-owned, MD-only telehealth practice operating in 41 states plus Washington, DC, and no nurse practitioners or physician assistants treat children here. A parent or legal guardian must be present and provide consent for every visit. Following American Academy of Pediatrics and American Academy of Ophthalmology guidance that most cases are self-limited, TeleDirectMD holds its antibiotic prescribing rate for diagnosed pediatric bacterial conjunctivitis in the 55 to 70 percent range and reserves topical antibiotics for cases that meet bacterial criteria. Self-pay visits are $79, and TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances.

whatIsCondition.sectionTitle: What Is Pink Eye in Children?
paragraphs: Pediatric conjunctivitis (pink eye) is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the clear membrane covering the white of the eye and the inner eyelid. Per the CDC, conjunctivitis is caused by viruses, bacteria, allergens, contact-lens use, chemicals, or fungi, and most acute infectious conjunctivitis is self-limited and does not require antimicrobial treatment.

Bacterial conjunctivitis is relatively more common in young children than in adults and typically produces thick, purulent discharge with matted lashes in the morning. Viral conjunctivitis usually causes watery discharge, often with a cold, while allergic conjunctivitis causes intense itching in both eyes with other allergy symptoms. A landmark systematic review by Azari and Barney (JAMA 2013) found that most conjunctivitis is self-limited.

TeleDirectMD focuses on uncomplicated pink eye in children ages 5 to 17 that is well-suited for video assessment, with a parent present, and refers children with eye pain, vision changes, light sensitivity, trauma, contact-lens-related red eye, or any conjunctivitis in an infant under 3 months to in-person or emergency care.

causesAndRiskFactors.sectionTitle: Causes and Risk Factors in Children
causesAndRiskFactors.intro: Pediatric pink eye in children ages 5 to 17 has several recognized causes and contributors:

items.label: Viruses:
items.text: the most common cause, often alongside a cold; usually self-limited.

items.label: Bacteria:
items.text: organisms such as Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus, more common in young children, typically with thick purulent discharge.

items.label: Allergens:
items.text: pollen, dust, and pet dander cause allergic conjunctivitis, which is itchy and not contagious.

items.label: Irritants:
items.text: smoke, chlorine, and chemicals can inflame the conjunctiva.

items.label: Contact with an infected person:
items.text: viral and bacterial conjunctivitis are highly contagious and spread quickly in schools and daycare.

causesAndRiskFactors.closing: Not every red eye is conjunctivitis. Foreign body or corneal abrasion, periorbital or orbital cellulitis, and a blocked tear duct can mimic pink eye. TeleDirectMD uses history and video exam to distinguish conjunctivitis from look-alike conditions and directs red-flag presentations to in-person evaluation.

compareCards.title: Viral vs Bacterial Conjunctivitis
compareCards.text: Viral conjunctivitis usually causes watery discharge, often affects both eyes, and frequently accompanies a cold; it is self-limited and does not benefit from antibiotics. Bacterial conjunctivitis produces thick purulent discharge with lashes matted in the morning and is more common in young children. The character of the discharge is the most useful distinguishing feature.

compareCards.title: Allergic Conjunctivitis vs Infection
compareCards.text: Allergic conjunctivitis causes intense itching in both eyes, is seasonal, and comes with other allergy symptoms such as sneezing and a runny nose. It is not contagious and is managed with antihistamine eye drops and allergen avoidance rather than antibiotics, which is why distinguishing it from infection matters for stewardship.

differentialDiagnosis.closing: If your child has eye pain, vision change, light sensitivity, trauma, or a contact-lens-related red eye, TeleDirectMD will direct you to in-person eye care rather than treating by video.

treatmentOptions.intro: Treatment depends on the cause. Viral and mild allergic conjunctivitis are managed supportively, and allergic conjunctivitis may be treated with an antihistamine eye drop. When the history and video exam support bacterial conjunctivitis, a TeleDirectMD physician may prescribe a topical antibiotic. Topical antibiotics are reserved for cases meeting bacterial criteria, and school or daycare return notes are provided where appropriate.

sections.title: Viral conjunctivitis
sections.text: Managed supportively with cool compresses, gentle cleansing of discharge, and hand hygiene. Most viral pink eye resolves over one to two weeks without antibiotics, per CDC guidance.

sections.title: Bacterial conjunctivitis
sections.text: When the discharge is thick and purulent with morning crusting and the picture supports a bacterial cause, a topical antibiotic such as erythromycin ointment, polymyxin B/trimethoprim, sulfacetamide, or tobramycin drops may be prescribed. Most schools allow return 24 hours after starting antibiotic drops and once drainage stops.

sections.title: Allergic conjunctivitis
sections.text: Itchy, bilateral, seasonal symptoms are managed with antihistamine eye drops and allergen avoidance. Allergic conjunctivitis is not contagious and does not require antibiotics.

sections.title: Red-flag presentations
sections.text: Eye pain, vision change, light sensitivity, trauma, contact-lens-related red eye, or any conjunctivitis in an infant under 3 months are referred to in-person or emergency eye care. TeleDirectMD does not prescribe steroid eye drops.

homeCare.sectionTitle: Home Care, Recovery Timeline, Prevention, and Follow-up

whatToDoNow.title: Timeline and What to Do Now
items: Apply a cool, clean compress and gently wipe discharge from the inner corner outward.
Wash hands frequently and avoid sharing towels or pillows to limit spread.
Discard eye makeup and do not wear contact lenses until symptoms fully resolve.
Most viral pink eye improves over 1 to 2 weeks without antibiotics.

whatToWatch.title: What to Watch For During Treatment
items: If eye pain, light sensitivity, or vision change develops, seek in-person eye care.
If swelling spreads to the eyelid or face or fever develops, seek urgent care.
If symptoms do not improve after the expected timeline, follow up or seek in-person care.
If a bacterial antibiotic is prescribed, most schools allow return after 24 hours of treatment and once drainage stops.

followUp.title: Prevention and Follow-up
items: Encourage frequent handwashing and avoid touching or rubbing the eyes.
Do not share towels, pillows, or eye drops between children.
Replace eye makeup that was used during an eye infection.
Keep the child home until any indicated therapy is started and drainage stops, per CDC.
Return for in-person care if there is eye pain, vision change, or no improvement.

items.question: Can TeleDirectMD treat my child's pink eye online?
items.answer: Yes, in most cases. TeleDirectMD treats pediatric conjunctivitis (pink eye, ICD-10 H10.9) by video visit for children ages 5 to 17 with a parent present. An MD distinguishes viral, allergic, and bacterial causes and prescribes treatment when indicated. The self-pay visit is $79, available in 41 states plus Washington, DC.

items.question: What is TeleDirectMD's antibiotic prescribing rate for children's pink eye?
items.answer: TeleDirectMD holds its antibiotic prescribing rate for diagnosed pediatric bacterial conjunctivitis in the 55 to 70 percent range, consistent with American Academy of Pediatrics and American Academy of Ophthalmology guidance that most cases are self-limited. Because many children diagnosed with pink eye actually have viral or allergic conjunctivitis, TeleDirectMD physicians reserve topical antibiotics for cases meeting bacterial criteria in children ages 5 to 17.

items.question: What ages does TeleDirectMD treat for pediatric pink eye?
items.answer: TeleDirectMD treats pediatric pink eye starting at age 5 and through age 17. All pediatric conditions begin at age 5, except acne, which begins at age 12. Any infant under 3 months with eye redness or discharge is a medical emergency requiring in-person evaluation, not telehealth, because of the risk of serious neonatal eye infection.

items.question: How can a doctor tell if pink eye is bacterial or viral over video?
items.answer: TeleDirectMD physicians distinguish bacterial from viral or allergic conjunctivitis in children ages 5 to 17 using history and a close video exam: thick purulent discharge with morning crusting suggests bacterial, watery discharge with a cold suggests viral, and intense itching with other allergy symptoms suggests allergic. Per CDC, most acute infectious conjunctivitis is self-limited and does not require antibiotics.

items.question: Will TeleDirectMD give a school or daycare return note for pink eye?
items.answer: Yes. TeleDirectMD provides school or daycare return notes for children ages 5 to 17 treated for conjunctivitis when appropriate. Per CDC, children may return once any indicated therapy is started and they have clinician approval; many schools allow return 24 hours after starting antibiotic drops and once drainage stops. CDC does not require exclusion unless the child has systemic illness.

items.question: What eye drops can TeleDirectMD prescribe for pediatric pink eye?
items.answer: For bacterial conjunctivitis in children ages 5 to 17, TeleDirectMD physicians can prescribe erythromycin 0.5% ophthalmic ointment (all ages), polymyxin B/trimethoprim drops (Polytrim, ages 2 months and older), sulfacetamide 10% drops, or tobramycin drops. TeleDirectMD does not prescribe steroid eye drops, which require a slit-lamp examination, and reserves antibiotics for cases meeting bacterial criteria.

items.question: When should pink eye be treated in person instead of online?
items.answer: See in-person care, not TeleDirectMD, if a child ages 5 to 17 has eye pain, light sensitivity, vision changes, eye trauma, or is a contact-lens wearer with a painful red eye, since these can signal a corneal ulcer or other serious condition. Any infant under 3 months with eye redness or discharge needs emergency evaluation rather than a video visit.

items.question: Does a parent need to be present for a child's pink eye visit?
items.answer: Yes. A parent or legal guardian must be present for the entire visit and provide consent for any child ages 5 to 17 seen by TeleDirectMD for pink eye. The guardian's identity is verified, and the child must be physically located in one of the 41 states plus Washington, DC where TeleDirectMD is licensed at the time of the visit.

items.question: How much does an online pink eye visit cost for a child?
items.answer: An online pediatric pink eye visit at TeleDirectMD costs $79 self-pay, no insurance required, for children ages 5 to 17. TeleDirectMD is in-network with Aetna, select Blue Cross Blue Shield plans, and UnitedHealthcare where applicable, but is not in-network with any Medicaid, Managed Medicaid, CHIP, or Medicare-Medicaid plan in any state.

items.question: Is pink eye in children contagious, and for how long?
items.answer: Yes. Per CDC, both viral and bacterial conjunctivitis are very contagious and spread through hand-to-eye contact, contaminated objects, and respiratory droplets; allergic conjunctivitis is not contagious. TeleDirectMD counsels parents of children ages 5 to 17 to wash hands often, avoid sharing towels, and discard eye makeup. Children may return to school once any indicated therapy is started and drainage stops.

paragraphs: This page is informational and is not a substitute for in-person medical care. TeleDirectMD treats children ages 5 to 17 for pink eye; we do not treat children under age 5 for any condition (ages 0 to 4 are excluded). A parent or legal guardian must be present for the entire visit and provide consent, and the child must be physically located in a licensed state (41 states plus Washington, DC) at the time of the visit.

TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances, steroid eye drops, or isotretinoin, does not diagnose or treat mental health conditions or ADHD, and does not make new asthma diagnoses. Any infant under 3 months with eye redness, discharge, or fever requires emergency care. TeleDirectMD is not in-network with any Medicaid, Managed Medicaid, CHIP, or Medicare-Medicaid plan in any state.
